title: More Than Just the Eyes

patient.name: Mr Rajendran s/o Muniandy
patient.presenting_complaint: Routine follow-up for diabetic eye screening, referred from polyclinic

history.hpc: Mr Rajendran is attending for a routine diabetic eye screening follow-up, referred from his polyclinic. He has no new visual complaints. The PSA is taking his general health history as part of the standard pre-consultation work-up. He mentions he recently started a new blood pressure medication and isn't sure of its name, only that it is 'a small white tablet'.
history.pmhx: Type 2 diabetes mellitus for 12 years. Hypertension for 8 years, medication recently changed by polyclinic doctor 2 weeks ago. High cholesterol on medication. No previous eye surgery. No known drug allergies.
history.family_hx: Father had diabetes and passed away from a stroke. Mother had hypertension.
medications: A new blood pressure tablet — name unknown, started 2 weeks ago, taken once daily
history.social_hx: Taxi driver, drives long hours daily. Smokes about 5 cigarettes a day for over 20 years. Drinks alcohol occasionally on weekends.

examination_findings.fundus: Not assessed at this stage — doctor to review for diabetic retinopathy screening

history_summary.systemic_conditions: Type 2 diabetes (12 years), hypertension (8 years, recent medication change), hyperlipidaemia
history_summary.medications: Metformin, an unidentified new antihypertensive (started 2 weeks ago), atorvastatin, aspirin
history_summary.action_taken: Patient advised to check the name and dosage of his new blood pressure medication (e.g., bring the box or a list from the pharmacy) for the doctor's reference; flagged to doctor that medication name is currently unknown

diagnosis: General health history taken as part of pre-consultation work-up for diabetic eye screening follow-up. Key points for doctor: long-standing diabetes and hypertension with a recent (2-week-old) antihypertensive medication change of unknown name, current smoking history, and aspirin use. History recorded for doctor review prior to fundus examination.

immediate: Confirm patient identity and explain that, before his eye check, you will ask some general health questions that help the doctor understand his overall condition
Ask about systemic conditions, particularly vascular conditions relevant to eye health: diabetes, hypertension, high cholesterol, heart disease
For diabetes, ask about duration and any recent blood sugar control information he may know (e.g., recent HbA1c if he recalls)
Ask about all current medications, including prescription, over-the-counter, and supplements — note that he is unsure of the name of his new blood pressure medication
Specifically ask about anti-coagulants or antiplatelet medications (relevant for any future procedures) — note his aspirin use
Ask about known drug allergies, including any eye drop allergies
Ask about smoking and alcohol use as part of social history
Ask about family history of relevant conditions (diabetes, hypertension, stroke, glaucoma, cataracts)
Advise Mr Rajendran to bring the box, strip, or a medication list for his new blood pressure tablet to his next visit, or to check with his pharmacy/polyclinic before then
Document all information accurately and flag the unidentified new medication for the doctor's attention
follow_up: Hand the completed history form to the doctor before the consultation
Clearly flag the unidentified new antihypertensive medication as an outstanding item
Ensure VA results are also available alongside the history for the doctor's review
patient_education: Encourage Mr Rajendran to always carry an updated medication list or bring his medication boxes to all medical appointments, including eye clinic visits
Remind him that smoking can affect eye health, particularly in the context of diabetes — but do not provide detailed counselling, as this is for the doctor
Reassure him that the doctor will review his full history along with his eye examination results today

key_points: Confirms patient identity and explains the purpose of the general health history questions
Systematically covers systemic conditions, especially vascular ones (diabetes, hypertension, cholesterol)
Asks about all medications including supplements, and identifies anti-coagulant/antiplatelet use (aspirin)
Asks about allergies, smoking, and alcohol use as part of a complete social/medical history
Recognises the gap created by the patient not knowing his new medication's name and takes a practical step (advise him to bring the box/list)
Documents duration of diabetes and hypertension as relevant background for diabetic retinopathy screening
Records family history relevant to eye conditions
Ensures VA results are paired with the history for the doctor's review
Does not attempt to identify or guess the name of the unknown medication
Flags the recent medication change and unknown medication clearly for the doctor, recognising its potential relevance
Does not provide any clinical interpretation of the diabetes/hypertension history to the patient
Recognises smoking and long-standing diabetes as relevant background for the doctor without diagnosing
Documents the full history accurately and completely
Hands the completed history to the doctor with the unidentified medication clearly flagged
Gives the patient practical, actionable advice (bring medication list/box) without overstepping into clinical counselling
Maintains a respectful, unhurried approach appropriate for a patient with multiple chronic conditions
